extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including standards for predictability, rationale to combine references, reliance on scientific theory or common knowledge, and examples of ordinary engineering choices. Aimed at how examiners should formulate and support obviousness rejections and how applicants may rebut them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some degree of predictability required; evidence of no reasonable expectation of success may support nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness does not require absolute predictability, but at least some degree of predictability is required; evidence showing there was no reasonable expectation of success may support a conclusion of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law: In re Rinehart (reversal where there was no reasonable expectation that combining prior art steps could be scaled up); Amgen, Inc. v. Chugai Pharmaceutical Co. (testimony supported no reasonable expectation of success in biotech); Ex parte Blanc (prior art teaching of efficient antioxidant supported reasonable expectation). Use factual and evidentiary showings to determine whether reasonable expectation of success existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability is determined at the time the invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an art is predictable or whether a proposed modification/combination had a reasonable expectation of success is determined as of the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the knowledge and expectations that one of ordinary skill would have had at the relevant time (Ex parte Erlich). Do not use hindsight knowledge gained after the invention date.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered when judging patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: "All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art." If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then claims depending therefrom are nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Wilson; also In re Fine re: dependence. Do not ignore claim language or selectively compare only some claim limitations to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered and cannot simply be disregarded
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation which is considered indefinite cannot be disregarded. If a claim admits more than one interpretation, and at least one interpretation renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, the examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and should also reject over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Ionescu (claims reversed as indefinite only); compare In re Wilson and In re Steele. Do not rely on speculative assumptions about claim meaning when making a 103 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations lacking support in the original specification must still be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating claims for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, all limitations must be considered and given weight, including limitations which do not find support in the specification as originally filed (i.e., new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disregard negative or other limitations absent from the original spec when determining obviousness (Ex parte Grasselli). Ensure the examiner's analysis accounts for such limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale to modify/combine prior art may be explicit in a reference or reasoned from common knowledge/scientific principles/legal precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to modify or combine the prior art does not have to be expressly stated in the prior art; it may be expressly or impliedly contained in the prior art or reasoned from knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill, established scientific principles, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must present a convincing line of reasoning supporting the rejection (In re Fine; In re Jones; In re Eli Lilly; In re Nilssen; Ex parte Clapp; Ex parte Levengood). Mere assertion without explanation is generally insufficient. Use the most appropriate source(s) of rationale and explain applicability to the facts at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of some advantage is the strongest rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest rationale for combining references is recognition, expressly or impliedly in the prior art or via a convincing line of reasoning based on established scientific principles or legal precedent, that some advantage or expected beneficial result would be produced by their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An implicit motivation to combine exists where the combination yields a more desirable, technology-independent improvement (e.g., stronger, cheaper, faster, smaller, more durable, more efficient). Courts have found that improving commercial opportunities by making a product/process better can supply motivation to combine even absent explicit suggestion in references (In re Sernaker; Dystar Textilfarben v. C.H. Patrick). Nevertheless, examiners should explain why such improvement would have been expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent can provide supporting rationale only when factual similarity exists
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may use the rationale used by a court in a prior legal decision if the facts in that decision are sufficiently similar to those in the application under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply precedent consistently, but do not rely solely on case law where the applicant has demonstrated criticality of a limitation. Courts provide a spectrum of illustrations; ensure the facts are sufficiently analogous before invoking precedent (In re Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale different from applicant's stated purpose is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage or result discovered by applicant; motivation to combine can be based on a general problem rather than the specific problem solved by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior art need not address the identical problem to motivate combination (In re Kahn; Cross Med. Prods. v. Medtronic; In re Linter; In re Dillon). Show that the art provided motivation to make the claimed compositions or combinations in expectation of similar properties or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure: consider inferences a person skilled in the art would reasonably draw
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering the disclosure of a reference, it is proper to take into account not only specific teachings but also the inferences which one skilled in the art would reasonably be expected to draw from the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases such as In re Preda and In re Lamberti to justify reading implied teachings (e.g., temperature ranges, implied substituents). Explain why the inference is reasonable and supported by the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on scientific theory requires evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner relies on a scientific theory to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, evidentiary support for the existence and meaning of that theory must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO must provide evidence supporting any chemical/technical theory invoked; e.g., In re Grose (no chemical theory existed to support prima facie obviousness of zeolite crystal forms). Cite In re Soli for permissible reliance on logic/scientific principle but accompany with evidence when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and standards for relying on common knowledge or taking official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may take official notice of facts or rely on common knowledge in the art only in limited circumstances; such instances should be rare and only where the facts are capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration as being well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A. Determine appropriateness: Official notice without documentary evidence permissible only when facts are instantaneously demonstrable; examples: In re Ahlert, In re Fox. Do not take notice for esoteric technical facts—these require documentary support (In re Ahlert, In re Grose, In re Eynde). B. If notice is taken, the technical line of reasoning must be clear and unmistakable; provide specific factual findings and sound technical reasoning so applicant can adequately traverse the rejection. C. If applicant challenges the assertion, the examiner must support the finding with adequate evidence (e.g., documentary evidence or an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.104(d)(2)). D. If a newly cited reference is later added only to support the prior common-knowledge finding and does not introduce new issues, the next Office action may be made final; otherwise it may not be final. E. Summary: judicious application; never rely solely on common knowledge as the principal evidence for a rejection (Zurko).

rubrics_metrics.name: When official notice is taken, provide explicit basis so applicant can traverse
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner takes official notice of a fact, the basis for doing so must be explicitly set forth so the applicant can adequately traverse the assertion in the next reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older cases accepted official notice where facts were readily verifiable or supported by other references; when taking notice, set forth the factual basis and reasoning (Soli; Chevenard). If applicant traverses adequately, examiner must produce documentary evidence in the next Office action to maintain the rejection (37 CFR 1.104(c)(2); Zurko).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic design changes: ornamentation without mechanical function generally not patentable distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters relating to ornamentation alone, which have no mechanical function, generally cannot be relied upon to patentably distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, courts have found exceptions where shape/ornamentation produces a product distinct from the reference (Ex parte Hilton). Evaluate whether ornamentation yields a functional or patentably significant difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the element's function is not desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Deletion of an element (and thereby its function) from a prior art reference is an obvious expedient where the function attributed to such element is not desired or required in the claimed context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Wu (omitting polybasic acid salts where their function not needed in certain environments); In re Larson; In re Kuhle. Show that omission would have been an expected design choice where the function was unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element with retention of the element's function is an indicia of unobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If an element is omitted from a claimed invention but the function of that element is nonetheless retained (by other features), that omission can indicate unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Edge (elimination of intermediate layer while retaining its protective function by alternative structure supported unobviousness). Consider whether eliminating an element while preserving function shows insight contrary to the art's expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in shape/configuration are often obvious absent persuasive evidence of significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Configuration or shape changes that are matters of choice are generally obvious unless there is persuasive evidence that the particular configuration is significant or produces unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Dailey: shape/configuration of disposable container was a matter of choice and found obvious. Applicant must show why configuration is critical or produces unexpected advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating a manual activity is not sufficient to distinguish over prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity which accomplishes the same result is generally not sufficient to distinguish over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Venner (automatic release replacing manual core release was not sufficient). Explain why automation yields new/ unexpected results if relying on it for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in sequence/order of steps are prima facie obvious absent new or unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of any order of performing process steps or mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious in the absence of new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Ex parte Rubin; In re Burhans; In re Gibson. If applicant claims particular sequencing, require evidence that the order yields unexpected or critical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in size/proportion (mere scaling) do not establish patentability absent different performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of relative dimensions or mere scaling up of a prior art device/process that does not produce different performance is not sufficient to patentably distinguish the claimed device/process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Rose (scale difference not sufficient); Gardner v. TEC Systems (relative dimensions alone not patentable if no performance difference); In re Rinehart (mere scaling up is not patentability). Applicant must show new or unexpected results from size/proportion changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous is often an obvious engineering choice unless showing unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations such as making something portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous are generally matters of ordinary engineering choice and not sufficient by themselves to establish nonobviousness unless they produce new or unexpected results or run contrary to art expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A. Making portable: portability alone not sufficient (In re Lindberg). B. Making integral: often an engineering choice (In re Larson), but may be patentable if it eliminates a known problem (Schenck v. Nortron). C. Making separable: obvious if desirability is evident (In re Dulberg). D. Making adjustable: adjustability where needed is not patentable (In re Stevens). E. Making continuous: converting batch to continuous operation can be obvious (In re Dilnot). Provide evidence of unexpected advantages to rebut obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal, duplication, or rearrangement of parts is prima facie obvious absent new/ unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal, duplication, or rearrangement of parts is typically an obvious expedient unless the change yields a nonobvious advantage or otherwise departs from the expectations of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law in this section illustrate that mere reordering or duplication of known parts is usually prima facie obvious. Examiners should require a showing of unexpected results or criticality to sustain patentability based on such changes.
